t: Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus in Weimar in 1919 to bring all the arts together and to train artists to work with industry.
Driven out of Weimar in 1925 and Dessau in 1932, the school was closed by its own leadership in Berlin in 1933 under pressure from the Nazis, whose writers had labelled it “un-German”.
Its émigré teachers carried its ideas to Britain, the United States and Tel Aviv, and its preliminary course became a common feature of design schools in many countries.
dyk: The most profitable product of the Bauhaus, a school remembered for its chairs and buildings, was its wallpaper.
ev: Walter Gropius founds the Bauhaus in Weimar, merging the Grand Ducal Saxon Academy of Fine Art and the Grand Ducal Saxon School of Arts and Crafts
The Bauhaus exhibits the experimental Haus am Horn, and László Moholy-Nagy takes over the preliminary course from Johannes Itten
After the Thuringian government halves its funding, the school moves to Dessau, where Gropius’s new building opens in late 1926
Gropius resigns and Hannes Meyer becomes director
The school turns its first profit under Meyer’s leadership
The mayor of Dessau, Fritz Hesse, dismisses Meyer, and Ludwig Mies van der Rohe takes over
The Nazi-led city council closes the Dessau school, and Mies moves it to a derelict factory in Berlin
After the Gestapo shuts the Berlin school, Mies and the faculty agree to close it themselves

f.where: Germany: Weimar (1919–1925), Dessau (1925–1932) and Berlin (1932–1933); afterwards carried by emigrants to Britain, the United States (Chicago, Harvard) and the White City of Tel Aviv
f.period: Weimar, 1919–1925, under Walter Gropius, with Johannes Itten’s preliminary course to 1923; Dessau, 1925–1932, under Gropius to 1928, Hannes Meyer 1928–1930 and Ludwig Mies van der Rohe from 1930; Berlin, 1932–1933, closed by its own leadership in 1933 under pressure from the Nazi regime
f.figures: Walter Gropius, founder and director 1919–1928; Hannes Meyer, director 1928–1930, a radical functionalist; Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, director 1930–1933; teachers Johannes Itten, Lyonel Feininger, Gerhard Marcks, Oskar Schlemmer, Paul Klee, Wassily Kandinsky, Gunta Stölzl and László Moholy-Nagy; Marcel Breuer, designer of the Wassily Chair
f.outcome: closed in 1933; its teachers and students spread its ideas abroad, through the New Bauhaus in Chicago, Harvard and the International Style; its preliminary course became a model for design schools; four of its sites in Germany became UNESCO World Heritage sites in 1996, two more in 2017
